1: The Azure Machine Learning workspace is the top-level container that centrally holds and governs all ML assets (datasets, models, environments, components). You must create it first before you can register or manage anything in it. A registry (A) and endpoints (C) come later; a Foundry project (D) targets generative AI, not traditional ML asset management.
2: Managed compute with autoscaling isolates each training workload while scaling to zero when idle, giving both isolation and cost control. Shared or fixed-size clusters cause resource contention or waste, and a dedicated cluster per experiment is not cost-aware.
4: Low-priority (Spot) VMs with discounted pricing are supported on Azure Machine Learning compute clusters. ACI and AKS do not offer low-priority pricing for this scenario, and local deployment has no VM discount.
5: Blue/green traffic splitting on an online endpoint routes a small percentage to the new deployment so you can validate it before shifting all traffic, with no disruption to existing users. Batch endpoints are not for real-time users, and replacing or routing all traffic is risky.
6: Azure OpenAI fine-tuning requires training data in JSON Lines (JSONL) format, one JSON example per line. CSV, TSV and plain JSON are not accepted.
7: Fine-tuning training files must be encoded as UTF-8. Other encodings (ASCII, UTF-16, ISO-8859-1) can corrupt tokens and special characters used in multi-turn chat data.
8: Fine-tuning begins with preparing labeled data as a JSONL file of prompt-completion pairs and uploading it. Prompt flow, deploying an endpoint, and enabling tracing are later or unrelated steps.
9: Fairness toward protected groups is assessed by comparing error rates across defined demographic cohorts (A), and prediction transparency across segments comes from feature importance (B). Latency and schema checks (C, E) are not Responsible-AI measures, and a single global cohort (D) hides group-level disparities.
10: A single pipeline with two triggers (a weekly schedule plus a data-drift alert) meets both needs without duplicating pipeline logic. Two pipelines duplicate logic, and functions or notebooks are manual.
11: Turning on Tracing for the prompt flow in Foundry captures the inputs, outputs, token usage and latency for each run, which is exactly what the goal requires. So the solution meets the goal (Yes).
12: A Git repository gives centralized versioning, history and reuse of shared prompt templates across projects. Embedding prompts in config files, registering them as datasets, or dropping them in blob folders lacks proper version control and reuse.
14: Building threshold checks as conditional logic inside the pipeline automatically gates registration and deployment to only models that pass, fully within the ML workflow. PR checks, Monitor alerts, and manual gates are not fully automated in the workflow.
15: The prompt flow SDK can enable tracing (start_trace) which captures inputs, outputs, token usage and latency per run, the same capability as the portal toggle, so it also meets the goal (Yes). [Corrected from the PDF, which marked No.]
17: Private endpoints place the workspace on a private IP and remove public internet access entirely. Service endpoints, NSGs and firewall rules restrict traffic but do not fully remove public accessibility the way a private endpoint does.
19: Adding a data/schema-validation component catches upstream schema changes and blocks invalid data before it reaches training, which is automated and robust. Ignoring differences, retraining manually, or using larger compute do not prevent bad data.
22: Without changing the embedding model, retrieval improves by adding an optimized re-ranker (B) and tuning chunk size and overlap to match content structure (D). Increasing token limits (A) raises cost, and changing vector length (C) means changing the embedding model.
23: Coherence measures how well a response reads and flows and needs no external reference or knowledge base, matching the constraint. Relevance, Similarity and QA-style evaluators rely on context or ground truth, which is not allowed here.
24: gpt-4o is the multimodal model that accepts both text and image input and supports fine-tuning. davinci-002, gpt-35-turbo and base gpt-4 do not fit the text+image fine-tuning requirement.
30: Fluency evaluates grammatical correctness and language quality of generated text. Coherence measures logical flow, Groundedness measures source support, and Similarity measures closeness to a reference.
31: Azure ML uses MLflow to consistently track parameters, metrics and artifacts across runs, ensuring reproducible, comparable experiment results. Job output logs, Application Insights, and Monitor alerts do not provide standardized experiment tracking.
33: Without labels you cannot compute accuracy, so data drift detection monitors shifts in the input data distribution to flag model-health problems continuously. Disabling monitoring or relying on manual evaluation is not continuous, and accuracy metrics need labels.
35: Batch endpoints are built for high-volume, non-latency-sensitive scoring of millions of records and scale cost-efficiently. Online and local endpoints target low-latency single requests, and notebooks do not scale.
36: Full private networking for Foundry requires disabling public network access (D) and configuring a managed virtual network (E) so managed services can still reach dependent Azure resources privately. Disabling all inbound access (A) breaks functionality, and a separate subscription (B) or API keys (C) do not provide network isolation.
37: Least privilege is enforced with built-in RBAC roles: platform engineers get the resource-level Azure AI Administrator role (B) to manage settings, and developers get the Azure AI Developer role (D) to build project assets but not change resource configuration. Shared API keys or disabling Entra ID weaken security.
38: The post-processing ThresholdOptimizer adjusts decision thresholds after training to improve fairness without retraining the model. ExponentiatedGradient and GridSearch are reductions that retrain, and CorrelationRemover is a preprocessing step.
39: Pinning specific model versions plus approval workflows prevents accidental deployment of the wrong version and enforces governance. Renaming models, increasing logging, or storing models locally do not control versions.
40: Setting a minimum instance count above zero keeps warm instances so the endpoint does not cold-start after scaling to zero, cutting latency spikes with minimal extra cost. Timeouts and logging do not fix cold starts, and batch endpoints are not real-time.
41: Reproducibility across regions and workspaces depends on versioned datasets and environments (pinned dependencies), not on identical hardware SKU, dataset name, or user identity.
42: The Content safety evaluator detects hateful and harmful content in model output, exactly the validation required before user exposure. Protected material, groundedness and indirect-attack evaluators target other risks.
45: Independent feature-engineering steps can run in parallel to cut overall runtime without changing any logic. Reducing data or combining steps changes behavior, and bigger compute does not parallelize sequential steps.
46: Full reproducibility requires versioning all three: code, dataset and environment. Any single one alone (Git only, metrics only, or dataset versioning only) is insufficient.
47: Archiving the model version hides it from active use so it can no longer be deployed while retaining it for compliance review and rollback. Deleting or unregistering removes it, and archiving the dataset does not change the model's deployability.
49: An Azure Machine Learning registry shares validated assets (models, components, environments) across multiple workspaces without copying, with central governance and versioning. Git sync, pipeline components, or a shared environment do not provide cross-workspace registry sharing.
50: Registering the trained artifact as a Model asset provides versioning, lineage and governed reuse across projects. Components, environments and pipelines serve other purposes.
51: The fastest recovery is rolling traffic back to the last known-good (previous) deployment using blue/green. Deleting and redeploying is slow, and changing authentication or compute size does not fix a bad release.
52: Defining and reusing a consistent environment (pinned dependencies) across training and inference prevents dependency mismatches between GPU training and CPU serving. Using the same compute is not required, and bigger compute does not fix dependency issues.
53: Storing secrets in Azure Key Vault and accessing them through a managed identity keeps credentials out of code, logs and environment variables. Hardcoding, config files, or local encryption all risk exposure.
54: A step-level retry policy transparently recovers from transient compute failures without changing core logic or significantly raising cost. Bigger compute or manual runs do not address transient failures.
55: Traffic splitting sends a controlled percentage of production traffic to the new model for safe validation without disrupting users. A separate staging endpoint does not test real production traffic, and a registry version or evaluation script is not a rollout strategy.
58: An automated evaluation step in CI/CD (for example GitHub Actions) can run both built-in and custom metrics and fail the build to block releases that miss the quality threshold. Tracing, manual review, or latency monitoring do not automatically gate releases.
59: The Evaluation experience compares metric scores across variants but does not itself capture the raw inputs, outputs, token usage and latency traces the goal requires (that is what Tracing does), so it does not meet the goal (No).
60: The model registry provides versioning, lineage, governance and discoverability/reuse of approved models across projects. Blob containers, Git, or a data lake lack model-specific governance.
61: Answers that are accurate and supported by sources are measured by Groundedness (A), and answers related to the user prompt are measured by Relevance (B). Harmfulness, Fairness and Tone do not measure answer reliability and meaningfulness for this goal.
62: The command uses the wrong script name (train.py instead of script.py) and passes the literal word training_data instead of the dataset path via an input binding, so it does not meet the goal (No).
64: Running script.py with the Azure ML input binding ${{inputs.training_data}} correctly passes the dataset path as a parameter value at job submission, so it meets the goal (Yes).
66: Passing a hardcoded positional filename (dataset1.csv) does not bind the training_data input parameter, so it does not meet the goal (No).
68: In the SDK v2 Environment class, the image parameter specifies the base Docker image. conda_file adds packages, build is for a Dockerfile build context, and properties holds metadata.
69: For low-latency real-time access shared across business units, a Standard (real-time) deployment such as Data Zone Standard is appropriate. The Batch types add latency, and Developer is for testing with a limited SLA.
70: Notebook/kernel state is reset by stopping the current kernel (B), resetting the compute (C), or changing the current kernel (E); each clears execution state. Changing compute or navigating away (A, D) do not reset the kernel state.
72: A hyperparameter sweep (tuning job) automatically runs many trials with different parameter values without editing the training script for each run. The other options are manual or happen after deployment.
109: Azure Blob Storage locations are referenced with the wasbs:// (Windows Azure Storage Blob, secure) URL scheme. hdfs, nfs and file are not blob schemes.
111: To align a GPT model with the requirements you apply Supervised fine-tuning (A) to adapt behavior and Evaluations (B) to measure quality and groundedness before and after changes. Guardrails and synthetic data generation do not by themselves align model performance to the stated requirements.
114: A folder that contains a CSV is loaded into a Pandas data frame with mltable.from_delimited_files(). from_parquet_files and from_delta_lake are for other formats, and load() opens an existing MLTable definition.
115: When real conversations cannot be used for compliance reasons, a simulator generates synthetic prompt-response interaction data matching the target task for fine-tuning. Evaluation logs and live traffic are not allowed or appropriate, and telemetry traces are not training pairs.
116: Create a hyperparameter tuning (sweep) job that runs multiple trials with different parameter values automatically. Manually changing values or duplicating the script does not automate tuning, and tuning after deployment is wrong.
117: Comparing embedding vector dimensions before and after a change does not measure answer groundedness or quality, so it does not evaluate whether RAG answer quality improved (No).
122: Reviewing subjective user-feedback comments is not a supported, measurable evaluation technique for groundedness or answer quality, so it does not meet the goal (No). [Corrected from the PDF, which marked Yes.]
123: For predictable, sustained high-volume traffic with strict SLAs, provisioned throughput with spillover traffic management absorbs excess demand and avoids throttling while keeping latency consistent. Increasing batch size, optimizing prompts, or serverless endpoints do not guarantee sustained capacity.
126: Determining what to do to get a desirable outcome is answered by the Counterfactuals component (A), and identifying the features with the most direct effect on the outcome is the Causal component (C). Error analysis and explanation answer different questions.
127: The scoring/entry script (its init and run functions) loads the model and uses it to return predictions from input data. Creating a Conda environment, registering the model, starting nodes, or specifying compute size are not the entry script's role.
129: Cloning an existing workspace is not a source-controlled, automated, repeatable deployment method (no infrastructure-as-code or versioning), so it does not meet the goal (No).
132: Manually creating workspaces in the Azure portal for each environment is not automated, repeatable or auditable through source control, so it does not meet the goal (No).
134: For efficient large-scale training and iterative development, configure an Azure Machine Learning compute cluster (C) for scalable training and register the data as a tabular dataset (D) for versioned reuse. JSONL conversion, an ADF schedule, and a single-node compute instance do not fit large-scale training.
137: Token throughput and average response latency measure performance, not answer quality or groundedness, so they do not evaluate whether the RAG quality change helped (No).
140: Numerical metrics are logged with mlflow.log_metric() (called per value or step to record a list of values). log_artifact and log_image are for files, and log_batch is not the standard per-metric method here.
141: Send 10% of traffic to the new deployment and use monitoring alerts on latency and error rate to trigger automatic rollback. Separate or batch endpoints and manual testing do not provide controlled rollout with automatic rollback.
142: A workspace managed identity authenticates to the Git repository centrally, so developers do not need to store personal access tokens locally and credential spread is reduced. Shared deploy keys, PATs in variables, or local authentication all spread credentials.
143: Enabling tracing and logging lets you inspect each workflow and pinpoint where and why response generation terminates early in production. A pre-release evaluation, changing max_tokens/temperature, or swapping models does not identify the production cause.
145: Azure ML Bayesian sampling supports only the choice, uniform and quniform distributions; for a continuous learning_rate the valid options here are Choice (A) and Uniform (B). QNormal, LogUniform and Normal are not supported by Bayesian sampling.
155: Bayesian sampling improves by learning from previously completed trials, so lowering max_concurrent_trials (to 4) improves sampling convergence. Raising it to 20 hurts convergence, and slack_factor tunes early termination, not sampling convergence.
156: Creating a feature Git branch for each prompt change lets you test and review new prompt versions safely without affecting production. A GitHub Action workflow or reverting production does not provide isolated experimentation.
159: Because advanced techniques should be applied only when needed, you first evaluate the model output to establish a baseline before fine-tuning or generating synthetic data. Deploying to production to gather feedback is not the first step.
